::: {.callout-warning}
Education only. Not for diagnosis, treatment or any clinical decision.
:::

## In 60 seconds

Computed tomography (CT) sends X-rays through the body along many lines and measures how much of each beam is
lost. Each measurement is a line integral of the attenuation coefficient; reconstruction turns a full set of them,
a sinogram, into slices. Hounsfield units (HU) put water at 0 and air at −1000. At the 60 keV used in this module,
blood and myocardium differ by about 5 HU, so the chambers are filled with iodinated contrast first. The heart
moves, so cardiac CT keeps only data from a short window of the cardiac cycle, about half a gantry rotation with
one X-ray source and a quarter with two [@petersilka2008; @mergen2023]. Before ablation, CT shows atrial and
venous anatomy, thrombus in the appendage [@romero2013], the course of the esophagus [@tsao2005] and wall thickness
[@beinart2011]; in ventricular tachycardia (VT), wall thinning has been studied as a marker of isthmuses
[@ciaccio2024; @moore2024]. Merged with the map, a surface fit reported 2.3 mm of error [@kistler2006], and in
dogs, ablation at CT-marked targets missed by 1.8–2.7 mm [@dong2006].

## From the field

- **Thrombus and predictive value.** Against transesophageal echo (TEE), CT detected appendage thrombus with 96%
  sensitivity and 92% specificity across 19 studies, but at a pooled prevalence of 8.9% only 41% of positive scans
  were true thrombus. With a delayed scan the figures were 100%, 99% and 92% [@romero2013]. Prevalence matters as
  much as the scanner (m35, m48).
- **Where the esophagus runs.** In 48 patients with AF, the esophagus touched the middle of the posterior left
  atrium in every one. In 42 its lower part ran close to the left inferior pulmonary vein (mean shortest distance
  2.8 mm), in 6 close to the right inferior vein [@tsao2005].
- **Walls thinner than the blur.** Left atrial wall thickness on CT averaged 1.89 mm and ranged from 0.5 to
  3.5 mm [@beinart2011]: the same order as the blur of the image, so how it is measured changes the answer (lab
  parts F and G).
- **Wall thickness and VT isthmuses.** In 61 patients with repaired tetralogy of Fallot (a congenital heart
  defect), median wall thickness at anatomical isthmuses was 2.6 mm where conduction was blocked, 4.8 mm where it
  was slow and 5.6 mm where it was normal [@moore2024]. In 6 patients with VT after infarction, the wall near the
  isthmus was a few hundred micrometers thick, and regions with the largest relative change in thickness partly coincided
  with the isthmus boundaries [@ciaccio2024]. Both are small single-center studies.
- **Faster windows, sharper images.** In 30 patients scanned at a 0.25-s rotation, reconstructions with a 66-ms
  window had fewer motion artifacts and sharper vessels than 125-ms ones [@mergen2023].
- **Reported error is not target error.** A surface fit to the map reported 2.3 ± 0.4 mm against 6.4 ± 2.8 mm for
  landmarks [@kistler2006]; that is a distance between surfaces. In dogs with markers sewn to the heart, the error
  at the targets themselves was 1.8–2.7 mm by chamber [@dong2006].

## Derivations

### Attenuation and Hounsfield units

A beam of intensity $I_0$ that crosses tissue with linear attenuation coefficient $\mu$ leaves with
$I = I_0 e^{-\int \mu\,ds}$ ([m49](m49-fluoroscopy-radiation.qmd#eq-m49-beer)). So one detector reading gives a
line integral, $p = -\ln(I/I_0) = \int \mu\,ds$. CT reports $\mu$ on a scale fixed by water ($\mu_w$) and air
($\mu_a$):

$$
\mathrm{HU} = 1000\,\frac{\mu - \mu_w}{\mu_w - \mu_a}
$$ {#eq-m51-hu}

Water is 0 and air is −1000 by construction; we take $\mu_a = 0$. With NIST mass attenuation coefficients at
60 keV [@nist126] (the same energy as m49), soft tissue is 54 HU, blood 59, fat −89 and cortical bone 1935 (lab
part A). Real CT beams contain many energies, so clinical values differ; the scale and the reasoning do not.

Blood and myocardium are 5 HU apart, too close to separate in a noisy image. Iodine attenuates far more
(7.579 cm²/g at 60 keV against 0.2059 for water [@nist126]), and attenuation adds by mass. A concentration $c$ in
mg/mL raises the value by

$$
\Delta\mathrm{HU} = 1000\,\frac{c \cdot 10^{-3}\,(\mu/\rho)_{\mathrm I}}{\mu_w}
$$ {#eq-m51-iodine}

with $(\mu/\rho)_{\mathrm I}$ in cm²/g and $\mu_w$ in 1/cm: 36.8 HU per mg/mL at 60 keV. The blood-pool
concentration in our phantom, 10 mg/mL, is illustrative.

**Key takeaways**

- A CT number is attenuation on a water-and-air scale; it depends on the beam energy.
- Contrast is what separates blood from myocardium.

### Projections and the central-slice theorem

Rotate the source and detector to angle $\theta$. The detector at offset $s$ records the integral of the image
$f(x, y)$ along the line $x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta = s$. The set of all such readings is the Radon transform
[@radon1986], drawn as a sinogram:

$$
p_\theta(s) = \iint f(x, y)\,\delta(x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta - s)\,dx\,dy
$$ {#eq-m51-radon}

For an ellipse of value $v$ the integral is $v$ times the chord, which has a closed form, so our phantom of
ellipses has an exact sinogram (lab part B). Take the 1-D Fourier transform of one projection and substitute the
line:

$$
P_\theta(k) = \int p_\theta(s)\,e^{-i2\pi k s}\,ds = \iint f(x, y)\,e^{-i2\pi k (x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta)}\,dx\,dy = F(k\cos\theta,\,k\sin\theta)
$$ {#eq-m51-slice}

This is the central-slice theorem: each projection gives the 2-D spectrum $F$ of the image along one line through
the origin. Enough angles fill the spectrum, and the image follows.

**Key takeaways**

- A sinogram is a stack of line integrals, one row per angle.
- Each row fills one line of the image's 2-D spectrum.

### Filtered back-projection

Write the inverse 2-D Fourier transform in polar coordinates. The area element $|k|\,dk\,d\theta$ brings in a
factor $|k|$, and with @eq-m51-slice:

$$
f(x, y) = \int_0^{\pi} q_\theta(x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta)\,d\theta, \qquad
q_\theta = \mathcal{F}^{-1}\{\,|k|\,P_\theta(k)\,\}
$$ {#eq-m51-fbp}

Filter each projection with the ramp $|k|$, then smear it back along its lines and add up the angles. Without the
filter, back-projection over-weights low frequencies and blurs the image. Sampled every $d$ mm and limited to the
detector's Nyquist frequency $1/(2d)$, the ramp becomes the Ram-Lak kernel [@kakslaney2001]:

$$
h[0] = \frac{1}{4d^2}, \qquad h[n] = -\frac{1}{\pi^2 n^2 d^2}\ \ (n \text{ odd}), \qquad h[n] = 0\ \ (n \text{ even},\ n \neq 0)
$$ {#eq-m51-ramlak}

It follows from $2\int_0^{1/(2d)} k\cos(2\pi k n d)\,dk$, which `tests/test_m51_ct.py` checks symbolically. With 180
angles our reconstruction puts the left atrium at 430 HU against a true 427 (lab part C).

::: {.demo #m51-d1 badge="simulation"}
```{=html}
<div id="m51-d1-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m51-d1"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m51-d1-sinogram.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: exact parallel-beam projections of an ellipse phantom (@eq-m51-radon), ramp-filtered with the Ram-Lak
  kernel (@eq-m51-ramlak) and back-projected with linear interpolation (@eq-m51-fbp); our own code, tested against
  `epml.ct`. Grid 160 × 160 pixels of 2 mm; one detector bin per pixel; 6–180 angles over 180°.
- Attenuation at one energy, 60 keV [@nist126]; lungs are drawn as air, and the iodine concentration (10 mg/mL),
  photon counts and all shapes are illustrative. Noise uses a normal approximation to Poisson
  counts (@eq-m51-noise).
- What would change the result: fan or cone beams, polyenergetic beams (beam hardening), scatter, detector blur,
  smoother filters, iterative reconstruction and motion, none of which are modeled.
:::

**Key takeaways**

- Back-projection alone blurs; the ramp filter undoes the blur.
- Too few angles leave streaks.

### Quantum noise and dose

Each ray ends in a photon count $N$ that is Poisson with mean $\bar N = N_0 e^{-p}$, where $N_0$ is the number of
photons sent along the ray. To first order,

$$
\operatorname{Var}\!\left[-\ln\frac{N}{N_0}\right] \approx \frac{1}{\bar N} = \frac{e^{p}}{N_0}
$$ {#eq-m51-noise}

Rays through more tissue are noisier. Reconstruction is linear, so image noise scales as $1/\sqrt{N_0}$, and dose
is proportional to $N_0$ (m49): halving the noise costs four times the dose. In lab part D the fitted slope of
log noise against log photon count is −0.51.

**Key takeaways**

- Noise falls with the square root of dose, not with dose.
- Thick or dense paths cost the most photons.

### ECG gating and motion

A slice needs projections over about 180°. With one X-ray source that takes about half a rotation; with two
source-detector pairs 90° apart, about a quarter [@petersilka2008]. For a rotation time $T_{\text{rot}}$ and
$N_{\text{src}}$ sources, the data window and the blur of a structure moving at speed $v$ are

$$
\Delta t \approx \frac{T_{\text{rot}}}{2\,N_{\text{src}}}, \qquad b = v\,\Delta t
$$ {#eq-m51-gating}

an approximation that ignores the fan angle and the details of how scanners weight their data. It gives 125 ms
and 62.5 ms at a 0.25-s rotation, against 125 and 66 ms reported [@mergen2023], and 82.5 ms at 0.33 s with two
sources, against 83 ms [@petersilka2008]. The ECG chooses where in the cycle the window sits.

Coronary arteries moved in plane at 46.6 mm/s on average, from 22.4 mm/s for the left anterior descending artery
to 69.5 mm/s for the right coronary artery, and slowest, 27.9 mm/s, at 48% of the cycle [@achenbach2000]. With a
125-ms window that is 5.8 mm of blur at the average speed and 3.5 mm at the slowest phase (lab part E). A disk of
diameter $D$ moving along $x$ by $b$ during the window is smeared into

$$
I(x, y) = \frac{\left|\,[x - b/2,\ x + b/2] \cap [-c,\ c]\,\right|}{b}, \qquad c = \sqrt{D^2/4 - y^2}
$$ {#eq-m51-smear}

the fraction of the window that the point $(x, y)$ spends inside the disk. Its peak is $\min(1, D/b)$: a 3-mm
vessel at 69.5 mm/s keeps 35% of its brightness with a 125-ms window.

::: {.demo #m51-d2 badge="approximate model"}
```{=html}
<div id="m51-d2-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m51-d2"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m51-d2-gating.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: @eq-m51-gating and @eq-m51-smear, a rigid disk moving at constant in-plane speed throughout the window;
  tested against `epml.ct`.
- Speeds are the published averages for coronary arteries [@achenbach2000]; rotation times of 0.25 and 0.33 s
  match the cited reports [@mergen2023; @petersilka2008], and values in between are illustrative. The vessel
  diameter is illustrative.
- What it ignores: speed changes within the window, motion along the scanner axis, the scanner's own spatial
  blur, data weighting and any motion correction. It is for intuition, not for predicting image quality.
:::

**Key takeaways**

- The window, not the rotation alone, sets the motion blur.
- A second source or a quieter phase of the cycle shortens the smear.

### Thin walls and wall thickness

Model the image blur as a Gaussian with full width at half maximum (FWHM) $\Gamma$, standard deviation
$\sigma = \Gamma/(2\sqrt{2\ln 2})$. A wall of thickness $w$ and unit contrast then reads

$$
g(x) = \tfrac12\left[\operatorname{erf}\!\left(\frac{x + w/2}{\sqrt2\,\sigma}\right) - \operatorname{erf}\!\left(\frac{x - w/2}{\sqrt2\,\sigma}\right)\right], \qquad
g(0) = \operatorname{erf}\!\left(\frac{w}{2\sqrt2\,\sigma}\right)
$$ {#eq-m51-wall}

Thickness read with a fixed threshold at half the contrast vanishes once $g(0) < 1/2$; read as the width at half
of the profile's own peak, it never drops below $\Gamma$. With an illustrative 1-mm blur, the thinnest published
left atrial wall, 0.5 mm [@beinart2011], reaches only 44% of its contrast: a half-contrast threshold misses it and
a FWHM reading gives 1.06 mm. The mean wall, 1.89 mm, reaches 97% and reads correctly (lab part F).

On a 3-D atrium the wall sits between blood and fat, not between two equal backgrounds, and voxels average
whatever they contain (the partial-volume effect). Segment the wall with a window between the fat-wall and
wall-blood midpoints. The blurred step from blood to fat passes through that window even where there is no wall
at all, over a width set by $\sigma$ alone: 0.61 mm at 1 mm of blur and 1.21 mm at 2 mm, from the same error
function as @eq-m51-wall (lab part G). So with 2 mm of blur the thinnest walls in lab part G (median 0.59 mm)
read 1.25 mm, about the width of the step itself. At 1.5-mm voxels the thinnest walls read one voxel, and on some
rays behind the atrium the window bridged the 3 mm of fat to the esophagus, so wall and esophagus read as one
structure. A distance transform of the segmented atrium gives the distance to the esophagus directly.

**Key takeaways**

- A wall thinner than the blur loses contrast before it loses width.
- Reported thickness depends on blur, voxel size and thresholds as well as on the wall.

### Merging CT with the map: two kinds of error

Registration itself is derived in m21; here we only read the evidence. A surface fit reports how far the map's
points lie from the CT surface: 2.3 ± 0.4 mm, against 6.4 ± 2.8 mm for pulmonary-vein landmarks, in 30 patients
[@kistler2006]. That number can be small even if the CT is shifted along the surface. In nine dogs with markers
sewn to the heart, ablation guided only by the registered CT landed 1.8–2.7 mm from the markers at autopsy,
depending on the chamber [@dong2006]. That is the error at a target, the quantity that matters for a lesion.
m55 builds an error budget from both.

**Key takeaways**

- Ask whether an error is between surfaces or at a target.
- Validation at a target needs an independent marker, such as one confirmed at autopsy.

## Clinical correlate

::: {.callout-note title="Pending clinical review"}
This section describes published findings only. It is not guidance for patient care, and it has
not yet been reviewed by an EP physician.
:::

**Where CT shows up in EP.** A European imaging and rhythm consensus document reviews CT alongside echo, MRI and
nuclear imaging for patients with AF and highlights its value in planning interventions [@donal2016]. The cited
studies use CT to look for appendage thrombus [@romero2013], to describe the course of the esophagus behind the
left atrium [@tsao2005], to measure atrial wall thickness [@beinart2011], to study wall thinning around VT
isthmuses [@ciaccio2024; @moore2024] and to merge anatomy with the map [@kistler2006; @dong2006].

**What the evidence is.** The thrombus figures come from a meta-analysis with TEE as the reference standard
[@romero2013]. The anatomy and wall-thickness studies are cross-sectional or small single-center cohorts
[@tsao2005; @beinart2011; @moore2024; @ciaccio2024]. The registration figures come from one clinical series and
one animal study [@kistler2006; @dong2006]. None of them is a trial of CT against no CT.

**What a reader should ask:**

- **Which phase and which window?** The atrium changes size and the esophagus moves; a scan is one moment.
- **Which resolution and which thresholds?** Thin walls and small distances depend on both (@eq-m51-wall).
- **Reported or target error?** A surface distance is not the error at a lesion [@kistler2006; @dong2006].

## How experts think

Before trusting a CT number or a measurement made on it, ask:

1. **What energy and what contrast?** Hounsfield units depend on the beam and on iodine
   (see @eq-m51-hu and @eq-m51-iodine).
2. **Was the motion frozen?** Compare the window with the speed of what you are measuring (@eq-m51-gating).
3. **Is the structure bigger than the blur?** If not, its contrast and its apparent size both
   change (@eq-m51-wall).
4. **How was it measured?** Threshold, voxel size and the neighbors of the structure all enter.
5. **Which error is quoted?** A surface distance after registration, or the error at a target
   [@kistler2006; @dong2006].

One sentence to keep: **a CT image is a reconstruction from line integrals at one moment, at one resolution, on a
scale set by water and air.**

## Cheat sheet

| Quantity | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Hounsfield units (@eq-m51-hu) | $1000(\mu - \mu_w)/(\mu_w - \mu_a)$; water 0, air −1000 |
| Iodine (@eq-m51-iodine) | $\Delta\mathrm{HU} = 1000\,c\cdot10^{-3}(\mu/\rho)_{\mathrm I}/\mu_w$; 36.8 HU per mg/mL at 60 keV |
| Projection (@eq-m51-radon) | $p_\theta(s) = \iint f\,\delta(x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta - s)$ |
| Central slice (@eq-m51-slice) | $P_\theta(k) = F(k\cos\theta, k\sin\theta)$ |
| Filtered back-projection (@eq-m51-fbp) | filter each projection with $|k|$, back-project over $[0, \pi)$ |
| Ram-Lak kernel (@eq-m51-ramlak) | $h[0] = 1/(4d^2)$; $-1/(\pi^2 n^2 d^2)$ for odd $n$; 0 for even |
| Noise (@eq-m51-noise) | $\operatorname{Var} \approx e^{p}/N_0$; image noise $\propto 1/\sqrt{\text{dose}}$ |
| Gating (@eq-m51-gating) | $\Delta t \approx T_{\text{rot}}/(2N_{\text{src}})$; blur $v\,\Delta t$ |
| Smeared disk (@eq-m51-smear) | peak $\min(1, D/b)$; length $D + b$ |
| Thin wall (@eq-m51-wall) | peak $\operatorname{erf}(w/(2\sqrt2\sigma))$; $\sigma = \Gamma/(2\sqrt{2\ln2})$ |

## Interview questions

Try each question before you open its model answer. In a real interview, say which assumptions you
are making.

**Q1. What does one CT detector reading measure?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The line integral of the attenuation coefficient along the ray, $-\ln(I/I_0) = \int\mu\,ds$
([m49](m49-fluoroscopy-radiation.qmd#eq-m49-beer)). All readings at all angles form the Radon transform of the
slice (@eq-m51-radon).

</details>

**Q2. Define the Hounsfield unit. Why can the same tissue read differently on two scanners?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

$\mathrm{HU} = 1000(\mu - \mu_w)/(\mu_w - \mu_a)$ (@eq-m51-hu). Attenuation depends on photon energy, and scanners
differ in tube voltage and filtration, so the beam spectrum differs. Reconstruction filters and calibration also
matter.

</details>

**Q3. Why does cardiac CT for mapping need contrast?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Blood and myocardium attenuate almost the same: at 60 keV they differ by about 5 HU (lab part A). Iodine adds
about 37 HU per mg/mL at that energy (@eq-m51-iodine), which separates the blood pool from the wall.

</details>

**Q4. State the central-slice theorem and say why it matters.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The 1-D Fourier transform of a projection at angle $\theta$ equals the 2-D Fourier transform of the image along
the line through the origin at that angle (@eq-m51-slice). It shows that projections at enough angles determine
the image, and it leads directly to filtered back-projection.

</details>

**Q5. Why does plain back-projection blur, and how does the ramp filter fix it?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Projections sample the 2-D spectrum along radial lines, densely near the center and sparsely far out, so plain
back-projection over-weights low frequencies (a point becomes a $1/r$ blur). The polar Jacobian $|k|$ restores
the weighting (@eq-m51-fbp). In practice the ramp is band-limited (@eq-m51-ramlak) and often smoothed to limit
noise.

</details>

**Q6. You halve the dose. What happens to the image noise?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

It rises by $\sqrt2$, about 41%, because noise scales as $1/\sqrt{N_0}$ and dose is proportional to
$N_0$ (@eq-m51-noise).

</details>

**Q7. What sets temporal resolution in cardiac CT, and how can it be improved?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The time to collect about 180° of data: roughly half a rotation with one source, a quarter with
two (@eq-m51-gating). Faster rotation and a second source shorten it; reported values are 125 and 66 ms at a 0.25-s
rotation [@mergen2023]. Choosing a quiet phase of the cycle lowers the speed instead [@achenbach2000].

</details>

**Q8. A vessel looks elongated and faint on a gated scan. Explain with numbers.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Motion during the window. At 69.5 mm/s and 125 ms it moves 8.7 mm, so a 3-mm vessel is smeared to about 11.7 mm
and keeps $3/8.7 \approx$ 35% of its peak brightness (@eq-m51-smear).

</details>

**Q9. Two groups report different mean left atrial wall thickness from CT. Give engineering reasons.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Different blur and voxel size, different thresholds or reading methods (fixed threshold against FWHM), different
cardiac phase, and different places on the wall. A wall near the blur width loses contrast and either vanishes or
reads too thick depending on the method (@eq-m51-wall); published walls are 0.5–3.5 mm [@beinart2011].

</details>

**Q10. A mapping system reports a registration error of 2 mm. Does that mean lesions land within 2 mm of where the CT says?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

No. The reported number is usually the distance between map points and the CT surface after the fit
[@kistler2006]; a shift along the surface does not change it. The error at a target must be measured with an
independent reference, as in the animal study that found 1.8–2.7 mm by chamber [@dong2006].

</details>

**Q11. How would you measure the distance from the posterior left atrium to the esophagus on CT?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Segment both, compute a Euclidean distance transform of the atrial segmentation and take its minimum over the
esophagus voxels (lab part G). State the phase, the voxel size and the thresholds, because partial volume can
merge the two when the fat between them is thin.

</details>

**Q12. CT found thrombus with 92% specificity. Why were most positive scans false positives in the meta-analysis?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Because thrombus was uncommon: at 8.9% prevalence, 96% sensitivity and 92% specificity give a positive predictive
value near 41% [@romero2013]. Predictive values depend on prevalence (m35); a delayed scan raised specificity to
99% and the positive predictive value to 92%.

</details>

## Code lab

The lab goes from tabulated attenuation to a reconstructed slice and ends with wall thickness on a 3-D atrium.

| Part | What you do | Data |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Hounsfield units and iodine (@eq-m51-hu, @eq-m51-iodine) | NIST attenuation tables |
| B | Projections and the central-slice theorem (@eq-m51-radon, @eq-m51-slice) | our own phantom |
| C | Filtered back-projection (@eq-m51-ramlak, @eq-m51-fbp) | our own phantom |
| D | Quantum noise and dose (@eq-m51-noise) | our own phantom |
| E | The gating window and motion blur (@eq-m51-gating, @eq-m51-smear) | published scanner and motion values |
| F | Thin walls under blur (@eq-m51-wall) | published wall thickness range |
| G | Wall thickness and esophagus distance on a 3-D left atrium | our own phantom |

- **Python notebook:**
  [labs/python/m51_lab.ipynb]({{< var repo.url >}}/blob/main/labs/python/m51_lab.ipynb).
  Run it from the course repository after `pip install -r requirements.txt`, or
  [open it in Google Colab]({{< var repo.colab >}}/blob/main/labs/python/m51_lab.ipynb).
- **Data:** published values as cited; everything else is generated by our own code. No downloads.

Each part ends with **checks**: lines that pass with the code as given. If you change something
and a check fails, that is information, not an error to hide.

## Self-check

Short checks you can do in your head. Open each answer after you have tried it.

**S1. A voxel has $\mu = 1.1\,\mu_w$. What is its CT number?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$1000 \times 0.1 = 100$ HU (@eq-m51-hu, with $\mu_a = 0$).

</details>

**S2. At 37 HU per mg/mL, what iodine concentration lifts blood by 300 HU?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

About 8 mg/mL (@eq-m51-iodine).

</details>

**S3. Every projection of an image has the same integral over $s$. Why?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

Integrating $p_\theta(s)$ over $s$ integrates $f$ over the whole plane, whatever the angle (@eq-m51-radon). It is
also the $k = 0$ value in @eq-m51-slice.

</details>

**S4. A single-source scanner rotates in 0.30 s. About how long is its half-scan window?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

About 150 ms (@eq-m51-gating).

</details>

**S5. You need half the noise. How much more dose, all else equal?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

Four times (@eq-m51-noise).

</details>

**S6. True or false: a wall thinner than the blur always looks thinner than it is.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

False. With a fixed threshold it may vanish; read as a width at half its own peak it looks at least as wide as
the blur, so thicker than it is (@eq-m51-wall).

</details>

## Literature figures

These sources are worth looking at alongside this module. We link to them instead of copying their figures: we
could not confirm a license that allows reuse here. Each entry says what to look for and where this module
explains it.

- **Filtered back-projection, from the source.** Kak and Slaney's book is free to read for personal use on the
  authors' site; see its chapter on reconstruction algorithms for nondiffracting sources and its chapter on
  aliasing artifacts and noise in CT images [@kakslaney2001;
  [electronic copy](https://engineering.purdue.edu/~malcolm/pct)]. This module: filtered back-projection.
- **Esophageal routes.** Tsao and colleagues classify the course of the esophagus by its nearest pulmonary vein and
  report the distances [@tsao2005; [article](https://doi.org/10.1378/chest.128.4.2581)]. This module: from the
  field.
- **Error at the target.** Dong and colleagues compare ablation sites with fiducial markers, chamber by chamber
  [@dong2006; [article](https://doi.org/10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.105.565200)]. This module: merging CT with the map.

## Further reading

- **Physics and reconstruction.** Radon's paper in translation [@radon1986]; filtered back-projection and its
  artifacts [@kakslaney2001]; attenuation data [@nist126].
- **Temporal resolution.** Two-source CT [@petersilka2008]; windows and image quality [@mergen2023]; coronary
  motion [@achenbach2000].
- **CT in EP.** Imaging in AF [@donal2016]; thrombus [@romero2013]; esophagus [@tsao2005]; wall thickness
  [@beinart2011; @moore2024; @ciaccio2024]; registration [@kistler2006; @dong2006].
- **Related modules.** m49 for X-ray attenuation and dose, m21 for registration, m40 for AI segmentation, m35 for
  predictive values, m48 for comparing modalities and m55 for an error budget across them.
